title: Working the Hit Parade in radio and early television
summary: Leeman did the Hit Parade on Saturday for $180, but Nick's would not let him off, so he quit and became a freelance New York studio musician for six and a half years.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Anyway, what I'm trying to drive at was I was offered the job on the Hit Parade, and I went up

for a week's trial, a couple week's trial, and I wanted to do the show. I was making, which was very good money -- Nick's paid jazz musicians better than any other places around, which was $170 or $175 a week at that time.

But I went in and rehearsed three days on Friday and did the Hit Parade on Saturday, with a three-or four-hour rehearsal, and made $180 for the two shows. We did first -- we rehearsed, and the Hit Parade went on as it had for years on the radio show coast to coast with the Hit Parade, and it was the first year of television.

And we would go on from the radio show and do the same show over again on television to the west coast, or vice versa -- I don't know which way around it was, which one we did first. We'd do the show twice. And they would not let me off at Nick's -- they would not let me off on Saturday night and be two hours late to work. So I couldn't do that show, and they would not let me send a sub in, so I quit and did my Hit Parade, which was the start of me working on the outside and becoming an outside musician.

Now I'm gonna answer your question before you get too far. During the interim, I was on that show for six and a half years, and many things transpired, which was the beginning of my career as an outside musician in New York.
